question: A 9-year-old child has typical absence seizures (3 Hz spike-and-wave on EEG). Which drug is first-line, and which commonly prescribed anticonvulsant is contraindicated?

answers.text: First-line: ethosuximide; contraindicated: carbamazepine — Na⁺ channel blockers paradoxically worsen absence seizures

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Ethosuximide selectively blocks T-type Ca²⁺ channels in thalamic relay neurons, interrupting the thalamocortical oscillation that generates absence seizures. Carbamazepine (and phenytoin) are Na⁺ channel blockers that worsen absence seizures by disrupting cortical-thalamic circuits — they are explicitly contraindicated.

answers.text: First-line: phenytoin; contraindicated: valproate — valproate causes hepatotoxicity in children

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Phenytoin is a Na⁺ channel blocker that worsens absence seizures — it is contraindicated, not first-line. Valproate is actually a valid alternative for absence seizures (especially when mixed with generalised tonic-clonic), though ethosuximide is preferred for pure absence.

answers.text: First-line: carbamazepine; contraindicated: ethosuximide — ethosuximide has no effect on generalised discharges

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is dangerously incorrect. Carbamazepine worsens absence seizures (it is a Na⁺ channel blocker, ineffective against T-type Ca²⁺ current). Ethosuximide is specifically designed for absence seizures — it targets the T-type Ca²⁺ channel responsible for the 3 Hz thalamocortical oscillation.

answers.text: First-line: levetiracetam; contraindicated: lamotrigine — lamotrigine causes fatal rash in children

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Levetiracetam is broad-spectrum but is not the established first-line for childhood absence epilepsy (ethosuximide and valproate have stronger evidence). Lamotrigine is actually a second-line option for absence seizures, not contraindicated — though it requires slow dose titration to avoid SJS.

overallFeedback.feedback: The most dangerous prescribing error in epilepsy is giving a Na⁺ channel blocker (phenytoin, carbamazepine) for absence seizures — these drugs worsen absence frequency. Always confirm seizure type before selecting an antiseizure drug.

The drug-seizure type matrix is a critical clinical tool: ethosuximide (T-type Ca²⁺ blocker) is first-line for pure absence; valproate for mixed absence + tonic-clonic. Na⁺ channel blockers (phenytoin, carbamazepine) are explicitly contraindicated in absence seizures.
